hops.title: Spiders straighten their legs with fluid pressure
hops.text: Spiders lack extensor muscles at their main leg joints, so the flexors that pull those joints inward have no muscle opposing them. To stretch a leg out, a spider contracts muscles in its front body section and pushes hemolymph into the leg under pressure, like hydraulic fluid. When a spider dies and that pressure vanishes, the flexors pull the legs inward, which is why dead spiders curl up. In 2022, mechanical engineers at Rice University put this to work. They pumped gentle air pressure into dead wolf spiders to open the legs, then released it so the legs closed on objects up to 130 percent of the spider's own mass.

sources.citation: Yap TF, Liu Z, Rajappan A, Shimokusu TJ, Preston DJ. Necrobotics: Biotic Materials as Ready-to-Use Actuators. Advanced Science. 2022;9(29):e2201174.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A fuzzy jumping spider on a green leaf stretching its front legs outward toward a dewdrop.
image.caption: Spiders straighten their legs by pushing hemolymph into them; without that pressure, the legs curl inward.

hops.afterHeading: Through the mammalian heart, valve by valve
hops.title: The ball-in-a-cage heart valve
hops.text: When surgeon Albert Starr teamed up with engineer Lowell Edwards, no published report described a patient living longer than three months with an artificial mitral valve. Their first designs copied natural flaps and failed. So they stopped imitating anatomy and built a cage holding a silicone rubber ball. Higher pressure behind the ball pushed it off its ring and let blood through; reversed pressure pressed it down to seal. It was first implanted in the mitral position in 1960. In a case reported in 2017, a Starr-Edwards aortic valve still worked normally 51 years after it went in, so surgeons left it. Its ball had been swapped once, early on.

sources.citation: Matthews AM. The development of the Starr-Edwards heart valve. Texas Heart Institute Journal. 1998;25(4):282-293.
Coselli JS. Durability Beyond Our Wildest Dreams: The Caged-Ball Valve at 60 Years. Texas Heart Institute Journal. 2022.
Amrane M, Soulat G, Carpentier A, Jouan J. Starr-Edwards aortic valve: 50+ years and still going strong: a case report. European Heart Journal - Case Reports. 2017.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage metal caged-ball heart valve with a white ball inside, resting on a wooden workbench beside calipers.
image.caption: A rubber ball in a metal cage opened and sealed with no power, pushed by the pressure difference across it.

hops.title: Giraffes do not have giant hearts
hops.text: People often repeat that a giraffe must have a giant heart to push blood all the way up its long neck. When researchers measured 56 giraffes from 18 to 1,500 kilograms, the heart averaged 0.51 percent of body mass, the same share as in other mammals. Giraffes do have about double the average arterial pressure of mammals their size, with peaks above 300 mmHg, and about double the vessel resistance. Instead of growing a huge heart, the giraffe's left ventricle has a thick muscular wall around a small inner cavity. That keeps the stress on the heart wall normal, but gives a smaller stroke volume for its body size.

sources.citation: Mitchell G, Skinner JD. An allometric analysis of the giraffe cardiovascular system. Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology Part A. 2009.

Smerup M, Damkjaer M, Brondum E, et al. The thick left ventricular wall of the giraffe heart normalises wall tension, but limits stroke volume and cardiac output. Journal of Experimental Biology. 2016.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A giraffe on a sunny savanna stretching its neck up to nibble leaves from an acacia tree, a small yellow bird nearby.
image.caption: A giraffe's heart is normal size for its body; a thick-walled left ventricle makes the extra pressure.

audio.title: A whale at two beats a minute, a wrong resistor, and hydraulic spiders
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories where the machinery of circulation shows up in places you would never expect.

First, how do you take an electrocardiogram on the largest animal that has ever lived? In Monterey Bay, California, a team of biologists steered a small inflatable boat up beside a single wild blue whale and reached out with a six-meter carbon-fiber pole to stick a suction-cup E C G tag onto it. The tag rode along for eight and a half hours, tracking feeding dives down to a hundred and eighty-four meters and as long as sixteen and a half minutes. When the whale dove deep, its heart slowed to four to eight beats a minute, and at its lowest dropped to just two beats a minute. That is thirty full seconds between one beat and the next. Its huge, stretchy aortic arch is thought to keep blood moving during those long pauses. Back at the surface after its deep dives, its heart usually raced at thirty to thirty-seven beats a minute, close to what the researchers estimated is the fastest a heart that big can beat. Scaling rules from other mammals predict that a seventy-thousand-kilogram blue whale has a heart of about three hundred nineteen kilograms, pushing roughly eighty liters of blood per beat. So while the whale recovers between deep dives, its rate dial is already turned nearly all the way up, and the team suggests limits like this may help explain why blue whales do not get even bigger.

Second, a lucky mistake with a parts box. In nineteen fifty-six, an electrical engineer named Wilson Greatbatch was teaching at the University of Buffalo and building an oscillator to help record rapid heartbeats. The circuit called for a ten-kilohm resistor. By his own account, Greatbatch reached into his resistor box, misread the color bands and plugged in a one-megohm one instead. When he switched it on, it fired a tiny electrical pulse lasting one point eight milliseconds, went quiet for one full second while drawing almost no current, and fired again. He stared at it in disbelief. That accidental rhythm was close to a resting human heartbeat, and he realized it could drive a human heart. He teamed up with two Buffalo surgeons, William Chardack and Andrew Gage. The three became known as the bow tie team: the doctors wore bow ties because children tend to pull long ties, and Greatbatch wore them so long ties would not get in the way when he soldered. On May seventh, nineteen fifty-eight, they touched two wires from their two-cubic-inch device to a dog's heart, and it beat in step. In June nineteen sixty, Chardack implanted one in a seventy-seven-year-old man whose heart's own conduction was blocked, and he lived uneventfully for two more years.

Third, shrink down from a blue whale to an open circulatory system. Spiders lack extensor muscles at their main leg joints; the flexors pull the legs inward. To straighten a leg, muscles in the spider's front body section squeeze hemolymph into the leg like hydraulic fluid. When a spider dies and that pressure is gone, its legs curl inward. In twenty twenty-two, mechanical engineers at Rice University realized that turns a dead wolf spider into a ready-made claw. By applying gentle pressure to open the legs and releasing it to close them, they picked up irregular objects weighing up to one hundred thirty percent of the spider's own mass. Same basic idea, bulk fluid under pressure, put to work in a wildly different way.
